SURAH "ṢĀD"

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ṣād.﴾ This letter from the letters of the alphabet is mentioned as a challenge and as an alert to the inimitability (i'jaz) of the Qur'an. Then He follows it with an oath whose answer is omitted, because the challenge indicates it. It is as if He said: ﴿By the Qur'an, possessor of the Reminder﴾, that is, possessor of honour, indeed it is an inimitable speech. It is also permissible that "Ṣād" is the predicate of an omitted subject, on the basis that it is the name of the surah, as if He said: "This is Ṣād," that is, "This is the surah which has rendered the Arabs incapable, and by the Qur'an, possessor of the Reminder," just as you say: "This is Hatim, by God," meaning: "This is the one famous for generosity, by God." Likewise, when He swears by it, it is as if He said: "I swear by Ṣād and by the Qur'an, possessor of the Reminder, that it is indeed inimitable." Then He said:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 2:

﴿Nay, but those who disbelieve are in arrogance﴾, pride that refuses to submit to this (Qur'an) and to acknowledge the truth,

﴿and opposition﴾, dissension against Allah and His Messenger. The indefinite form in "arrogance and opposition" is for indicating their intensity and their growing severity. It is also read "fi ghirrah" (فِي غِرَّةٍ), meaning: in heedlessness, of what is incumbent upon them of reflection and following the truth.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 3:

﴿How many We destroyed﴾: a warning to those who possess might and defiance.

﴿before them﴾: before your people.

﴿of a generation﴾: of a community.

﴿and they called out﴾: they supplicated and sought relief, when they saw the punishment.

﴿but no longer was there time for escape﴾: here "lā" (no) is the one resembling "laysa" (is not), to which the feminine ta' has been added, just as it was added to "rubba" (many a) and "thumma" (then), for emphasis. Its ruling has thereby changed: it only enters upon time-words (ahyan), and only one of its two governed elements appears, either the subject (ism) or the predicate (khabar), while the appearance of both together is prohibited. This is the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh. According to al-Akhfash, it is the "lā" of generic negation, to which the ta' has been added, and it is restricted to negating time-words. As for His words ﴿ḥīna manāṣ﴾ (the time of escape): "manāṣ" means refuge or deliverance, and it is in the accusative case governed by it, as though you had said, "and there is no time of escape for them." According to al-Khalil and Sibawayh, the accusative is based on the assumption of the phrase "wa-lāta ḥīna manāṣ," meaning "and the time is not a time of escape."

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verses 4–5:**

﴿And they wondered that there came to them﴾, that there came to them,

﴿a warner from among themselves﴾, a messenger from among themselves, warning them. That is, they found it far-fetched that the Prophet should be a human being.

﴿And the disbelievers said, "This is a sorcerer, a great liar. Has he made the gods one God? Indeed, this is a astonishing thing."﴾ He did not say "and they said," to express anger against them, and to indicate that this statement is not dared to be made except by the disbelievers who have plunged deeply into disbelief and are absorbed in error, for there is no disbelief more extreme than to call the one whom God has confirmed "a liar, a sorcerer," and to marvel at monotheism, which is the clear truth, while not marvelling at polytheism, which is vain falsehood. It is narrated that when ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, embraced Islam, the believers rejoiced at it and it grieved the Quraysh. So twenty-five of their chieftains gathered and went to Abu Talib and said: "You are our elder, and you know what these fools have done"—meaning those who had entered Islam—"and we have come to you so that you may judge between us and your nephew." Abu Talib summoned the Messenger of God ﷺ and said: "O nephew, these are your people; they ask you for fairness, so do not incline entirely away from your people." He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "What do they ask of me?" They said: "Leave us alone and abandon the mention of our gods, and we will leave you and your God." He ﷺ said: "Give me one word by which you will rule the Arabs, and by which the non-Arabs will submit to you." They said: "Yes, and ten [words]"—that is, we will give it to you and ten words with it. He said: "Say, there is no god but God." So they stood up and said: "Has he made the gods one God?! — that is, has he made them into one?—indeed, this is an astonishing thing," that is, (p-145) extremely strange in its wonder. It has also been said: "ʿAjīb" is that which has no like, and "ʿujāb" is that which has no like at all.

And the chiefs among them set off, saying: "Go on, and be steadfast in your worship of your gods. Indeed this is a thing that is intended."

Al-Nasafi's commentary (Madarik al-Tanzil) on this verse:

The chiefs of Quraysh left the assembly of Abu Talib after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had silenced them with a ready reply. They said to one another: "Go on" (ان امشوا). Here "an" is in the sense of "i.e." (ay), because those who leave a gathering of debate must necessarily speak with one another and discuss what has happened to them, so their departing included the sense of saying.

"And be steadfast in" (واصبروا على): in the worship of

"your gods" (آلهتكم). "Indeed this" (إن هذا): the matter

"is a thing that is intended" (لشيء يراد). That is, Allah (Exalted is He) intends it and decrees its execution, so there is no turning it back, and nothing helps in it except patience. Or, "this matter" is one of the calamities of the age, intended against us, so there is no escape for us from it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 7:

﴿We have not heard of this﴾, i.e., of tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness),

﴿in the latter religion﴾, i.e., in the religion of ʿIsa (Jesus), which is the last of the religions, because the Christians are trinitarian and do not affirm God's oneness; or in the religion of Quraysh, upon which we found our forefathers,

﴿This is nothing but an invention﴾ [Sad: 5], i.e., this is not (anything else),

﴿but a fabrication﴾, a lie that Muhammad (ﷺ) fabricated of his own accord.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 8:

﴿Has the Reminder been sent down to him, out of all of us?﴾ The Reminder is the Qur'an.

﴿Out of all of us﴾: they denied that he should be singled out for nobility from among their nobles, and that the Book should be sent down to him from among them, out of envy.

﴿Nay, they are in doubt about My Reminder﴾: that is, about the Qur'an.

﴿Nay, they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾: Nay, they have not yet tasted My punishment. When they taste it, the doubt and envy that are in them will be removed at that time. That is to say: they will not believe in it unless the punishment touches them, and then they will believe at that time.

Or do they possess the treasuries of your Lord's mercy, the Almighty, the Bestower?

That is, they do not own the treasuries of mercy, so that they might bestow it upon whomever they wish, withhold it from whomever they wish, and choose from among their own chieftains for prophethood, and set themselves above Muhammad (ﷺ) through it. Rather, the one who owns mercy and its treasuries is the Almighty (al-'Aziz), the Irresistible over His creation, the Bestower (al-Wahhab), the Abundant in gifts, the One who places it in its proper place, who distributes it according to what His wisdom requires. Then he reinforced this meaning, saying:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 10:

﴿Or do they possess the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them?﴾ (so that) they may speak about the divine affairs and the divine arrangements which belong exclusively to the Lord of might and majesty. Then He mocked them in the utmost manner of mockery, saying: If they are fit to manage creation and to dispose of mercy,

﴿then let them ascend by the means﴾, that is, let them climb the ladders and the paths by which one reaches the heaven, so that they may manage the affairs of the world and the kingdom of God, and send down revelation to whomever they choose. Then He promised His Prophet ﷺ victory over them, saying:

**Al-Nasafi, *Madarik al-Tanzil* (commentary on Surah 38, verse 11)**

﴿Jundun﴾ (a host), a *mubtada'* (subject of a nominal sentence),

﴿mā﴾ (what), a *ṣila* (an expletive particle, *ṣila*), which strengthens the indefinite noun that serves as the subject,

﴿hunālika﴾ (there), refers to Badr and the places where they fell, or to the place where they put themselves in the position of being sent out for such a great saying, from their saying to someone who is appointed to a task that is not his concern: "You are not there (*lasta hunālika*)." The predicate of the subject is ﴿mahzūmun﴾ (routed), meaning *maksūrun* (broken),

﴿mina l-aḥzāb﴾ (from among the factions), is connected to *jundun*, or to *mahzūmun*. The meaning is: "They are only a host from among the disbelievers who band together against the Messenger of Allah, who will soon be routed. So do not concern yourself with what they say, and do not be troubled by what they babble."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 12:

﴿They denied before them﴾, before the people of Makkah,

﴿the people of Nuh﴾, [they denied] Nuh,

﴿and ʿAd﴾, [they denied] Hud,

﴿and Pharaoh﴾, [he denied] Musa,

﴿the lord of the stakes﴾. It is said: he had stakes and cords with which he would play before himself. And it is said: he would peg whoever he tortured by four stakes, [fixed] in his hands and his feet.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 13:

﴿And Thamud﴾ - they are the people of Salih - (Salih),

﴿and the people of Lut﴾ (Lut),

﴿and the companions of the Thicket﴾ (al-Aykah), meaning the thick grove, (Shu'ayb),

﴿those are the confederates﴾. By this indication he intends to inform that the confederates whom the defeated army was made of, they are they, they are they, and that they are the ones among whom denial was found.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 14:

﴿Each of them merely denied the Messengers, so My punishment became due.﴾ He mentioned their denial first in a declarative sentence, in a general way (ʿalā wajh al-ibhām), without specifying who was denied. Then He came with the exceptive sentence (al-jumla al-istithnāʾiyya), which made it clear in it and specified who was denied, namely the Messengers. He mentioned that each one of the factions (al-aḥzāb) denied all of the Messengers, because in denying one of them there is a denial of all of them, given the unity of their call (li-ittiḥād daʿwatihim). In the repetition of the denial and its clarification after its generality, and in the variation in its repetition, first with the declarative sentence and second with the exceptive one, and in what the exceptive sentence contains of placing [the verb] in the manner of emphasis (al-waḍʿ ʿalā wajh al-tawkīd), there are kinds of intensification (al-mubālagha) that record upon them the deserving of the most severe and most eloquent punishment. Then He said: ﴿So My punishment became due﴾, meaning: therefore it was necessary that their punishment become due. "ʿadhābī" and "ʿiqābī" in both states (al-ḥālayn) — "Yaʿqūb".

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 15:

﴿And these do not await﴾, i.e., the people of Makkah do not await, and it is permissible that it refers to all the factions (al-ahzab),

﴿except one Shout﴾, i.e., the first blast (al-nafkhah al-ula), which is the Great Terror (al-fazaʿ al-akbar),

﴿for which there is no recovery﴾. It is read with a ḍammah (fawāq) by Ḥamzah and ʿAlī, meaning: there is no delay for it, not even the measure of a fawāq, which is the interval between the two milkings of the milker, i.e., when its time comes, it will not be delayed even this amount of time. And it is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both: "there is no return or repetition," from "afāqa al-marīḍ" when he returned to health. The fawāq of the she-camel is the moment in which the milk returns to her udder, meaning it is only one blast, not repeated, nor reiterated.

And they said, "Our Lord, hasten for us our *qiṭṭ* (قِطَّنا), our share of Paradise." Because he (peace be upon him) mentioned God's promise of Paradise to the believers, they said, mockingly: "Hasten for us our share of it, or our share of the punishment You promised," like His saying: ﴿And they ask you to hasten the punishment﴾ [al-Hajj: 47]. The origin of *qiṭṭ* (القِطّ) is *al-qist* (القِسْط), meaning a portion of a thing, because it is a piece of it, from "*qaṭṭahu*" (قَطَّهُ), meaning he cut it. The document of a reward or allotment is also called *qaṭṭ* (قَطّ), because it is a piece of the paper (*qirṭās*).

﴿Before the Day of Reckoning﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 17:

﴿Be patient over what they say﴾, concerning you, and guard yourself lest you slip in what you have been charged with of persevering with them and bearing their harm.

﴿And remember Our servant Dawud﴾, and his honour before Allah, how he slipped that slight slip, so he met with what he met of the punishment of Allah.

﴿Possessor of strength (dha al-ayd)﴾, possessor of strength in religion. This indicates that "al-ayd" means strength in religion. Its evidence is His saying: ﴿Indeed, he was one who often turned back (awwab)﴾, i.e., one who returns repeatedly to the good pleasure of Allah (Exalted), and this is an explanation of "dha al-ayd." It is related that he used to fast one day and break his fast the next day, and this is the most excellent fasting, and he would stand in prayer for half the night.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 18:

﴿Indeed, We subjected﴾, made submissive,

﴿the mountains to glorify [Allah] with him﴾. It was said: their subjection was that they would travel with him whenever he wished to move them to wherever he desired (p-148),

﴿glorifying﴾, in the sense of "glorifying [Allah] (musabbihat)", in the state of a circumstantial clause (hal). He chose "yusabbihna" over "musabbihat" to indicate that the glorification by the mountains occurred gradually, moment after moment, and state after state.

﴿in the evenings and at sunrise﴾, i.e., at the two ends of the day. "Al-ʿashiyy" (the evening) is the time from ʿasr until night, and "al-ishraq" (sunrise, the brightening) is the time of ishraq, which is when the sun shines (tushriq), i.e., gives light, and it is the time of al-duha (forenoon). As for shuruq (ushriq, the sun's rising), it is its rising. One says: "The sun has risen (sharaqat al-shams), but it has not yet shone (lamma tushriq)." It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "I did not know the prayer of al-duha except through this verse."

Qur'anic quotations: ﴿And the birds gathered together﴾.

And We subjected the birds, gathered together from every direction. And from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "When he [Dawud] glorified (Allah), the mountains responded to him with glorification, and the birds gathered around him and glorified (Allah), and that is their being gathered (mahshurah)."

﴿Each one of them was one who turned back in repentance (awwab) to Him﴾. Each one of the mountains and the birds, for the sake of Dawud, meaning: for the sake of his glorification, was glorifying (musabbih), because they used to glorify in response to his glorification. He placed awwab in the position of musabbih, because the awwab, which is the tawwab (one who repeatedly turns back), the one who frequently returns to Allah and seeks His good pleasure, is by his habit one who frequently mentions Allah and constantly glorifies and sanctifies Him. It was also said: the pronoun refers to Allah, meaning: each of Dawud, the mountains and the birds is, for Allah, awwab, that is, glorifying (musabbih), returning the glorification (murajji' lil-tasbih).

﴿And We strengthened his kingdom﴾: We made it strong. It was said: thirty-three thousand men would spend the night around his sanctuary (miḥrab), guarding him.

﴿And We gave him wisdom﴾: the Zabur (the Psalms), and knowledge of the sharā'i' (divine laws). It was also said: every speech that agrees with the truth is ḥikmah (wisdom).

﴿and decisive speech (faṣl al-khiṭāb)﴾: knowledge of judgment, ending disputes, and distinguishing between truth and falsehood. Al-faṣl means distinguishing between two things. It is said of clear speech that it is "faṣl," in the sense of "maf-ṣūl" (that which is separated), like "ḍarb al-amīr" (the ruler's striking). Faṣl al-khiṭāb is clear speech, summarized, which the one addressed understands clearly, so that it is not confused for him. It is also possible that al-faṣl has the sense of "al-fāṣil" (that which separates), like "al-ṣawm" and "al-zawr." The intended meaning of faṣl al-khiṭāb is then the speech that separates, which divides the sound from the corrupt and the truth from falsehood. This is his speech in cases, rulings, the administration of the kingdom, and consultations.

It is related from ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him): "It is judging by evidence (bayyinah) upon the claimant, and the oath upon the one who is accused." This too is among the separating between truth and falsehood.

It is related from al-Shaʿbī: "It is his saying, 'Ammā baʿd (now then),' and he was the first to say 'Ammā baʿd.' Whoever speaks on a matter of importance begins with the mention of Allah and His praise. Then, when he wishes to proceed to the purpose intended, he separates between that and the mention of Allah by saying, 'Ammā baʿd.'"

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 21:

﴿And has there come to you the news of the adversaries?﴾ Its apparent form is a question, and its meaning is an indication that it is among the wondrous reports. "Al-khasm" (the adversary, i.e. the litigant party) means "al-khusama'" (the disputants), and it applies to the singular and the plural, because it is originally a verbal noun (maṣdar); you say "khasamahu khaṣman" (he disputed with him).

The position of ﴿idh﴾ (when) is governed either by an omitted element, its estimated form being: "And has there come to you the news of the litigation of the adversaries?" or by "al-khasm" (the adversaries), because of the verbal sense it contains.

﴿They climbed over the sanctuary (tasawwarū al-miḥrāb)﴾: they ascended its wall and came down to it. "Al-sūr" (the wall) is the high wall; and "al-miḥrāb" (the sanctuary chamber) is the upper chamber, or the mosque, or the front part of the mosque.

﴿Idh﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the first ﴿idh﴾ in the previous verse.

﴿They entered upon Dawud, and he was alarmed by them﴾. It is related that Allah (exalted is He) sent two angels to him in the form of two men. They asked to enter upon him, but they found him on his day of worship. The guards prevented them, so they climbed over the mihrab (prayer niche) to him, and he did not notice until they were sitting before him.

﴿and he was alarmed by them﴾, because they had entered upon him at the mihrab on a day that was not a day of judgment, and because they had come down upon him from above, on a day of seclusion, while the guards surrounding him did not allow anyone to enter upon him.

﴿They said: "Fear not. Two adversaries"﴾. This is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), meaning: "We are two adversaries."

﴿"One of us has wronged the other"﴾, meaning he has transgressed and acted unjustly. ﴿"So judge between us with truth and do not deviate"﴾, meaning do not be unjust. It is from "al-shatat" (shatat), which is exceeding the limit and departing from the truth.

﴿"And guide us to the even path"﴾, meaning direct us to the middle of the road and its straight course. What is intended is the very essence of truth and its pure form.

It is related that the people of Dawud's time used to ask one another to give up their wives to them, so that they might marry them if they pleased them. This was a customary practice of mutual assistance. The Ansar used to share in this way with the Muhajirun. It so happened that Dawud (peace be upon him) cast his eye on the wife of Uriyya (Uriyya), loved her, and asked him to give her up to him. Uriyya was too shy to refuse, so he did so, and Dawud married her. She was the mother of Sulayman. It was said to him: "Despite your great station and your many wives, it was not fitting for you to ask a man who had only one wife to give her up to you. Rather, the duty upon you was to overcome your desire, to subdue your soul, and to be patient with what you were tested with."

It was also said: Uriyya proposed to her, then Dawud proposed to her, and her family preferred him. So his lapse was that he proposed over the proposal of his believing brother, despite his many wives. And what is related, that he sent Uriyya again and again to the expedition of al-Balqa', desiring that he be killed so that he could marry her, is not fitting for those who are marked by righteousness among the common Muslims, let alone for some of the great prophets.

Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Whoever narrates to you a story about Dawud (peace be upon him) as the storytellers (qussas) relate it, I will flog him one hundred and sixty times, which is the prescribed punishment (hadd) for slander (fira) against the prophets."

It is related that this was mentioned to Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, and a man of the people of truth was with him. He denied the narrator and said: "If the story is as it is in the Book of Allah, then it is not fitting to seek its opposite, and how great it is that anything else should be said. And if it is as you mention, and Allah withheld it as a veil over His Prophet, then it is not fitting to make it manifest about him." Umar said: "My hearing this speech is dearer to me than everything the sun has risen upon."

What the parable which Allah struck with his story (peace be upon him) indicates is nothing more than his request to the husband of the woman that he give her up to him, and no more. It came in the manner of parable (tamthil) and allusion (ta'rid), not explicit statement, because it is more effective in rebuke, since when reflection leads a person to perceive what is alluded to, it has a greater effect on the soul, firmer lodging in the heart, and greater impact upon it, while observing good manners by avoiding open declaration.

Indeed, this is my brother. It is either a substitute (badal) for "this" or the predicate of "inna." What is meant is brotherhood in religion, or brotherhood of friendship and familiarity, or brotherhood of partnership and mixing (khultah), in keeping with His words: "And indeed many of the partners (al-khulata')..." [Q 38:24 in part], "He has ninety-nine ewes, and I have one ewe." "Li" (I have), "Hafs" (a proper name), and "al-na'jah" (the ewe) is a metaphor for a woman. Since this is a depiction of the matter and a supposition of it, there is no impediment to the angels supposing it concerning themselves, just as you would say: "I have forty sheep, and you have forty, so we mixed them," and what belongs to the two of you of the forty is not four nor a quarter of them.

﴿Then he said: Commit her to me⦆ — i.e., make her mine (mallikniha). Its literal meaning is: "Make me responsible for her, just as I am responsible for what is under my hand." It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that it means: "Make her my share" (kifli), i.e., my portion.

﴿And he overpowered me⦆ — and he prevailed over me. It is said: "'azzahu" and "ya'izzuhu."

﴿in the speech⦆ — in the dispute. That is, he was more capable of argument than I. By "al-khitab" is meant addressing the one who argues and disputes, or it means: I proposed to the woman and he proposed to her, so he addressed me with a proposal, i.e., he overcame me in the matter of the proposal, so he prevailed over me, in that she was married to him rather than to me. The point of the parable is that the story of Uriah with David is depicted through the story of a man who had one ewe while his partner had ninety-nine; his companion wished to complete the hundred, so he coveted his partner's ewe and sought to make him leave its ownership and transfer it to him, and he argued with him in that matter with the argument of one eager to attain his aim. This was on the basis of their coming before him for judgment, so that he would rule by what he ruled by, from His words:

He said, "He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe be added to his ewes," so that he would be proven wrong by his own judgment. This is the answer to an omitted oath. This statement expresses disapproval of the action of his partner. The word *su'al* (demand) is a verbal noun (*masdar*) in a genitive construction, with its object following it. It has been given the meaning of *idafa* (addition, joining), so it takes the same complement that *idafa* takes. It is as if it were said: "by adding your ewe to his ewes," in the sense of asking and requesting. He wronged the other man only after his opponent had acknowledged it. The Qur'an does not relate this, because it is already known. It is related that he said: "I want to take her from him and complete my ewes to one hundred." Dawud said: "If you intend that, we will strike you on this and this," and he pointed to the tip of the nose and the forehead. The man said: "O Dawud, you deserve to be struck on this and this, for you did such-and-such and such-and-such." Then Dawud looked around and saw no one, and he understood what he had fallen into.

﴿And indeed many of the partners﴾, meaning the associates and companions,

﴿transgress against one another, except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾. The word *al-mustathna* (the exception) is in the accusative case, and it is of the same category as the thing excluded, and the thing excluded from is "*ba'duhum*" (some of them).

﴿And few are they﴾. *Ma* here is for vagueness (*ibham*, indefiniteness of quantity), *hum* is the *mubtada'* (subject), and *qalil* (few) is its *khabar* (predicate).

﴿And Dawud thought﴾, that is, he knew and became certain. The word *zann* (thought) is borrowed for this sense, because a strong *zann* comes close to knowledge.

﴿that We had tested him﴾, meaning We had tried him.

﴿So he asked his Lord for forgiveness﴾, for his slip.

﴿And fell down prostrating﴾, that is, he fell upon his face prostrating to Allah. In this is evidence that bowing (*ruku'*) takes the place of prostration in prayer if it is intended, because the purpose is merely what is suitable as humility at this recitation. The *ruku'* in prayer performs this function, unlike *ruku'* outside of prayer.

﴿and turned back﴾, meaning he returned to Allah in repentance. It was also said that he remained prostrate for forty days and nights, not raising his head except for the obligatory prayer or what was necessary, and his tears did not stop until grass grew from his tears, and he did not drink water except that two-thirds of it was tears.

﴿So We forgave him that﴾, i.e., his slip,

﴿and indeed for him with Us is nearness﴾, because of his closeness,

﴿and a good place of return﴾, a return (ma'ab), and it is Paradise.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 26:

﴿O Dawud, indeed We have made you a khalifa (vicegerent) on the earth﴾. That is: We have made you a successor (istakhlafna) in sovereignty over the earth. Or: We have made you a khalifa from among the prophets who came before you, who upheld the truth. In this is evidence that his state after repentance remained as it had been, unchanged.

﴿So judge between the people with truth﴾. That is: by the judgment of God, if you are His khalifa; or with justice.

﴿And do not follow desire﴾. That is: the desire of the self in your judgment,

﴿for it will lead you astray﴾, the desire,

﴿from the way of God. Indeed, those who go astray from the way of God﴾, that is His religion,

﴿for them is a severe punishment because they forgot the Day of Reckoning﴾. That is: because of their forgetting the Day of Punishment.

(p-153) "And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them" [from the creation] "in vain" (bāṭilan): a creation in vain, not for a sound wisdom; or [as a construction] of those who are void and playful (mubṭilīn ʿābithīn), like His saying: "And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in play" [al-Anbiya: 16]. Its underlying sense is "those possessing vanity" (dhawī bāṭilin), or "in play" (ʿabathan), so that "vain" (bāṭilan) is placed in its position. That is: We did not create them and what is between them for mere play and sport, but for the manifest truth, which is that We created souls, endowed them with reason, granted them capacity, removed their impediments, then exposed them, through obligation, to great benefits, and prepared for them an end and a recompense according to their deeds.

"That" (dhālika): a reference to their creation being in vain.

"The assumption of those who disbelieved" (ẓannu alladhīna kafarū): the word ẓann here carries the sense of "the object of assumption" (al-maẓnūn), that is: "that its creation is for play and not for wisdom is the assumption of those who disbelieved." They were made to be those who assume that He created it for play and not for wisdom, despite their acknowledgment that He is the Creator of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, in accordance with His saying: "And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say: Allah" [Luqman: 25]. For since their denial of the resurrection, the reckoning, the reward and the punishment led to the conclusion that the creation of it is play and vanity, they were treated as though they assume and say this, because recompense is that for which wisdom in the creation of the world was aimed; so whoever denies it has denied the wisdom in the creation of the world.

"So woe to those who disbelieved, from the Fire" [Sad: 27].

Qur'anic verse: ﴿Shall We make those who believe and do righteous deeds like the corrupters in the earth? Or shall We make the God-fearing like the wicked?﴾

"Am" (أمْ) is disjunctive (munqati'a), and the interrogative sense in it is one of denunciation (inkar). The meaning is that if the requital were void, as the disbelievers say, the conditions of the one who does good and the one who does evil, and of the one who is God-fearing and the one who is wicked, would be equal; and whoever equates between them would be foolish (safih) and would not be wise (hakim).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 29:

﴿A Book﴾: that is, this is a Book,

﴿which We have sent down to you﴾, meaning the Qur'an,

﴿blessed﴾: another attribute,

﴿that they may ponder its verses﴾. Its original form is "li-yatadabbarū" (liyatadabbaru), and it has also been read with this form. Its meaning: that they may reflect upon its verses, so that they may come to understand what is in it and act upon it. From al-Hasan: "This Qur'an has been recited by slaves and children who have no knowledge of its interpretation; they have memorized its letters and neglected its limits." "Li-tadabbarū" (with the second tā' of the verb being dropped as a result of the assimilation? no) — read in the second person (ʿalā al-khiṭāb), with one of the two tā's elided, as Yazid reads it.

﴿And that those possessed of minds may take heed﴾: and that people of intellect may be admonished by the Qur'an.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 30:

﴿And We bestowed upon Dawud Sulayman. An excellent servant!﴾ That is, Sulayman. It is said that it refers to Dawud, but this is not the correct view. The one being praised is thus omitted.

﴿Indeed, he was ever oft-returning (awwab).﴾ He gave the reason for his being praised as being that he was awwab, that is, one who returns much to Allah (Exalted is He).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 38, verse 31:

﴿When it was displayed before him﴾, before Sulayman,

﴿in the evening﴾, after midday,

﴿the swift-footed steeds﴾: the horses standing on three legs, while the other leg rests on the tip of its hoof.

﴿the prancing ones﴾: the swift ones. It is the plural of *jawad* (a fine, noble horse), because it is generous (*yajud*) in running. He described them with *al-subun* (standing still, poised), because it is not found in mixed-breed horses but only in purebred ones (*al-ʿirab*). It was also said: he described them with *al-subun* and *al-jawda* (swiftness and generosity) so that he might combine for them the two praiseworthy descriptions: standing still and running. That is, when they stand still they are calm and composed in their places, and when they run they are swift and light in their running. It was also said: *al-jiyad* means those with long necks, from *al-jid* (neck).

It is reported that Sulayman, peace be upon him, raided the people of Damascus and Nasibin and seized a thousand horses. It was also said that he inherited them from his father, and that his father had acquired them from the Amalekites. It was said that they came out of the sea, having wings. He sat one day after praying midday on his throne and reviewed them, and they continued to be displayed before him until the sun set, and he neglected the afternoon prayer, which was obligatory for him. He was distressed over what he had missed, so he took them back and slaughtered them, seeking nearness to God. Thus a hundred remained. Whatever horses are in people's hands are from their offspring. It was also said that when he slaughtered them, God replaced them with something better than them, which is the wind, running by his command.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 32:

﴿So he said, "Indeed, I have loved the love of good (al-khayr) over the remembrance of my Lord, until it [the sun] disappeared behind the veil."﴾ That is: I preferred love of horses over the remembrance of my Lord. So reports al-Zajjaj. Thus "ahbabtu" (I loved) is in the sense of "athartu" (I preferred), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Fussilat: 17], and "'an" (over) is in the sense of "'ala" (above). He called the horses "khayr" (good) as though they were the very essence of good, because good is attached to them, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Good is tied to the forereaching of horses until the Day of Resurrection." Abu 'Ali said: "Ahbabtu" is in the sense of "jallastu" (I made to sit down), from "ihbab al-ba'ir" (the making of a camel kneel), which is "burukuhu" (its kneeling). "Hubb al-khayr" means the wealth, and it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), with an attributive construction to the object.

﴿Until it disappeared﴾: the sun.

﴿Behind the veil﴾: What indicates that the pronoun refers to the sun is the prior mention of the evening (al-'ashiyy). A pronoun must have a preceding reference, or an indication of one. Alternatively, the pronoun refers to "al-safinat" (the swift steeds), meaning: ﴿until it disappeared behind the veil﴾ of the night, that is, the darkness.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 33:

﴿Bring them back to me.﴾ That is, he said to the angels: "Return the sun to me so that I may pray the afternoon prayer (ʿasr)." So the sun was returned to him, and he prayed the afternoon prayer. Or (it means): "Return the horses (al-ṣāfināt) to me."

﴿So he began to pass his hand over the shanks and the necks.﴾ He began to strike (masḥan), that is, he struck the sword against their shanks (sūq), the plural of sāq, like dār and dūr, and their necks (aʿnāq), meaning he cut them. This was because they had distracted him from the prayer. It is said: "masaḥa ʿilāwatahu" (he wiped his neck), when he struck his neck; and "masaḥa al-musaffir al-kitāb" (the scribe wiped the book), when he cut its edges with his sword. It is also said: he did this as an expiation for them, or in gratitude for the return of the sun. The horses were permitted as food in his law, so it was not a destruction (of property). It is also said: he wiped them with his hand, out of admiration for them and delight in them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 34:

﴿And indeed We tested Sulayman﴾, We tried him,

﴿and We placed upon his throne﴾, the throne of his kingship,

﴿a body; then he turned back (in repentance)﴾, he returned to Allah. It was said: Sulayman was tested after he had ruled for twenty years, and he ruled for twenty years after the trial. Among his trial was that a son was born to him, and the shayatin (devils) said: If he lives, we will not be free of forced labour (sukhra). So our course is to kill him or to harm him (nukhabbilahu, to make him mad/affect his mind). Sulayman, peace be upon him, came to know of this, so he would nurse him in the cloud, out of fear of the harm of the shayatin. Then his son was cast down dead upon his throne, and he became aware of his lapse in that he had not put his trust in his Lord regarding him. And it has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Sulayman said: Tonight I will go round to seventy women, each one of whom will bring forth a horseman who will fight in the way of Allah." He did not say: "If Allah wills." So he went round to them, and only one woman conceived, and she brought forth half a man. He was brought upon his throne (p-156) and placed in his lap. By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, had he said: "If Allah wills," they would all have fought in the way of Allah as horsemen."

As for what is related of the tale of the ring and the shaytan, and the worship of an idol in the house of Sulayman, peace be upon him, it is among the falsehoods of the Jews.

"My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom that will not belong to anyone after me." He placed seeking forgiveness (istighfar) before asking for a kingdom, following the practice of the prophets, peace be upon them, and the righteous, who place seeking forgiveness before making a request.

"It should not be" means it is not made easy and does not occur.

"For anyone after me" means besides me. Reading the ya' with a fatha, as Madani and Abu 'Amr did, gives "it should not be for anyone after me." He made this request in this manner so that it would be a miracle (mu'jizah) for him, not out of envy. Before that, the wind and the devils had not been subjected to him. When he made this supplication, the wind and the devils were subjected to him. It would not be a miracle unless it breaks the customary patterns (al-'adat).

﴿Indeed You are the Bestower.﴾

﴿So We subjected the wind to him﴾. "الرِّياحُ" (al-riyāḥ, "the winds"): Abu Ja'far (read it in the plural).

﴿flowing﴾: a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative, a word describing the state of the subject or object at the time of the action) of "الرِّيحَ" (al-rīḥ, "the wind").

﴿by His command﴾: refers to Sulayman.

﴿gently﴾: "لَيِّنَةً" (layyinatan, "soft"), "طَيِّبَةً" (ṭayyibatan, "pleasant"), "لا تُزَعْزِعُ" (lā tuza'za'u, "not violently shaken"). It is a ḥāl from the pronoun in "تَجْرِي" (tajrī, "flows").

﴿wherever﴾: a ẓarf (adverbial accusative of place) of "تَجْرِي" (tajrī, "flows").

﴿it struck﴾: "قَصَدَ" (qaṣada, "aimed at") and "وأرادَ" (wa-arāda, "and intended"). The Arabs say: "أصابَ الصَوابَ فَأخْطَأ الجَوابَ" (aṣāba al-ṣawāba fa-akhṭa'a al-jawāba), meaning: he hit the right point but missed the answer.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 37:

﴿And the devils﴾: a conjunction (ʿatf) upon "the wind" (al-rīḥ), meaning: We subjected to him the devils.

﴿every builder﴾: a substitute (badal) for "the devils." They would build for him whatever he wished of structures.

﴿and diver﴾: meaning, they would dive for him into the sea to bring out pearls. He was the first to extract pearls from the sea. The meaning is: "And We subjected to him every builder and diver from among the devils."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 38:

﴿And others﴾: an conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon "every builder" (kull bannāʾ), falling within the ruling of a substitute (badal),

﴿bound together in chains﴾: and he (Solomon) would bind the rebellious devils together with one another in fetters and chains, for discipline and to restrain them from corruption. And "al-ṣafd" means the fetter, and the word was also used for a gift, because it is a binding of the one who is benefited by it. From this is the saying of ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him: "Whoever does good to you has taken you captive, and whoever shuns you has set you free."

(p-157) ﴿This﴾, which We have given you of kingship, wealth and power, ﴿is Our gift, so bestow or withhold﴾: give from it whatever you wish of bestowal, which is the giving, or withhold from giving. He was rewarded when he gave, and if he withheld he did not sin, unlike others.

﴿without reckoning﴾ is connected to "Our gift." It was also said that it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: "This is Our gift in abundance and great quantity, such that it is hardly possible to count it." Or: this subjugation (of the devils) is Our gift, so bestow freedom upon whomever of the devils you wish, or ﴿withhold﴾ whomever of them you wish in chains, ﴿without reckoning﴾, that is, without any reckoning against you in that matter.

﴿وَإنَّ لَهُ عِنْدَنا لَزُلْفى وحُسْنَ مَآبٍ﴾ ﴿And indeed, for him is nearness to Us and a good return.﴾

"لَزُلْفى" is the ism (subject noun) of inna (the emphatic particle), and the khabar (predicate) is "لَهُ" (for him). The amil (governing element) in "عِنْدَ" ('inda, "with" or "near") is the khabar.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 41:

﴿And remember Our servant Job﴾: it is a substitute (badal) for "Our servant," or an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan). ﴿When﴾: a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from it.

﴿He called upon his Lord﴾: he supplicated Him.

﴿"Indeed, I have been touched by"﴾: "that I have been touched by," a quotation of his words with which he called out. Had he not quoted them, it would have said "that he had been touched by," because he is in the third person.

﴿Satan with hardship﴾: the reading of the common people (al-ʿammah) is "bi-nusbin." Yazid [read it] with the intensified form "nasabin," like "rushdun" and "rashadun." Yaʿqub [read it] "bi-nasbin," according to the original form of the verbal noun. Hubayrah [read it the same way]. The meaning is one: fatigue (al-taʿab) and hardship (al-mashaqqah).

﴿And torment﴾: he means his illness and the various kinds of distress he suffered from in it. It was also said: he meant what the Satan would whisper to him during his illness, magnifying the calamity that had befallen him and urging him toward aversion and impatience (al-jaza'). So he sought refuge in Allah that He would suffice him against that, by removing the affliction, or by granting him success in repelling and turning it back through patient forbearance (al-sabr al-jamil). It is narrated that three of the believers used to visit him. One of them apostatized, so he asked about him, and it was said: Satan had cast into his mind that Allah does not test the prophets and the righteous. It is also mentioned regarding the cause of his affliction that he slaughtered a sheep and ate it while his neighbor was hungry, or that he saw an evil and remained silent about it, or that Allah tested him to raise his ranks, without any prior lapse on his part.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 42:

﴿Strike with your foot⁠—﴾ This is a recounting of what Ayyub (peace be upon him) was answered with; that is, We sent Jibril (peace be upon him) to him (p-158), and he said to him, "Strike with your foot," that is, strike the earth with your foot, and it was the land of al-Jabiyah. So he struck it and a spring gushed forth, and it was said: ﴿This is a cool bath and drink﴾; that is, this is what you bathe in and drink from, and thereby your inward and outward state will be healed. It was also said: two springs gushed forth for him, and he bathed in one of them and drank from the other, and the disease departed from his outward and inward being, by the permission of Allah (Exalted).

Qur'anic quotations: "And We gave him his family and the like of them with them" — ﴿And We gave him his family and the like of them with them﴾.

Translation:

﴿And We gave him his family and the like of them with them﴾. It was said: God (exalted is He) revived them in their very persons, and increased him with the like of them.

﴿As a mercy from Us and a reminder for those of understanding﴾. It is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) for both. That is, the gift was for mercy to him, and for reminding those of understanding, because when they hear of what We bestowed upon him for his patience, it encourages them to be patient in the face of trial.

And take in your hand a bundle (ḍigth) of grass, and strike with it, and do not break your oath. (Verse 44)

[Note: the translation above is incomplete; the full passage follows below.]

Actually, let me give the complete translation as required:

﴿And take (wa-khudh)﴾, conjoined (ma'tuf) to "irkud" (strike with your foot).

﴿In your hand a bundle (ḍigth)﴾: a small bundle of grass, or of basil, or of something else. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "a handful of twigs."

﴿Then strike with it and do not break your oath﴾: He had sworn during his illness that he would strike his wife one hundred times once he recovered. So Allah dissolved his oath with the least burdensome thing for him and for her, because of the goodness of her service to him. This concession remains in effect, and each of the hundred strokes must reach the one being struck. The reason for his oath was that she was late in returning to him, having gone out on an errand, so his chest became constricted. It is also said that she sold her two braids for two loaves of bread, and they were the thing Ayyub (peace be upon him) would hold on to when he stood up.

﴿Indeed We found him﴾: We knew him,

﴿patient﴾: under trial. Indeed he complained to Allah of what afflicted him and asked Him for mercy, but complaint to Allah is not called impatience (jaza'). Ya'qub (peace be upon him) said: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah﴾ [Yusuf: 86]. Moreover, he (peace be upon him) was seeking healing out of concern for his people lest they fall into trial, since Satan was whispering to them that if he were a prophet he would not have been afflicted with what he was afflicted with, and out of desire for strength to obey. His condition reached the point that nothing remained of him except the heart and the tongue.

﴿How excellent a servant﴾: Ayyub,

﴿indeed he was one who turned back (awwab) [to Allah]﴾.

(p-159) ﴿And remember Our servants﴾ — "عَبْدَنا" (ʿabdanā, "Our servant"), read by Makkī (Ibn Kathīr) —

﴿Ibrahim, Ishaq and Yaʿqub﴾. Whoever reads it as a plural (ʿibādanā) makes "Ibrahim" and those after him an appositive (ʿaṭf bayān, explanatory apposition) to "ʿibādanā"; whoever reads it in the singular ("ʿabdanā") makes "Ibrahim" alone an appositive to it, and then he conjoins his descendants (dhurriyyatahu) to "ʿabdanā". Since most deeds are carried out by the hands, the hands were given precedence, so it is said of every deed: "This is from what their hands have done" (mimmā ʿamilat aydīhim), even if the deed is one in which direct action by the hands is not possible, or if the workers were amputees with no hands. On this basis the words ﴿possessors of hands and eyesight﴾ were revealed, meaning: possessors of manifest deeds and inner reflections. It is as if those who do not perform the deeds of the Hereafter, who do not strive in the cause of God, and who do not reflect on the thoughts of people of religions, are in the position of the disabled, who cannot use their limbs, and of those whose minds are taken away, who have no insight. This contains an implicit reproach against everyone who is not among the workers of God nor among those who have insight into the religion of God, and a rebuke for their abandoning striving and contemplation while being able to do both.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 46:

﴿Indeed, We purified them﴾: We made them sincere to Us (khalisin lana),

﴿with a pure quality﴾: with a quality that is pure, with no admixture in it,

﴿the remembrance of the Abode﴾: "ذكرى" (dhikra) is in a place of accusative or nominative case, by supposing "a'ni" (I mean) or "hiya" (it is), or in the genitive, as a badal (substitution in apposition) for "khalisa" (pure). The meaning is: "Indeed, We purified them with the remembrance of the Abode." "Al-dar" (the Abode) here means the Hereafter. That is, We made them sincere to Us by making them remind people of the Hereafter and make them abstain from the world, as is the habit (daydan) of the prophets, peace be upon them. Or its meaning is that they often mention the Hereafter and returning to God, and forget the mention of the world. "With a pure remembrance" in the idafa (construct) form is the reading of Madani (the reader from Medina) and Nafi' (Nafi' al-Madani, one of the canonical reciters), and it is an idafa of a thing to what clarifies it, because the pure thing is a remembrance, and other than a remembrance. "Dhikra" is a verbal noun (masdar) in idafa to the object, meaning: by their purifying the remembrance of the Abode. It has also been said: "khalisa" has the meaning of "khulus" (purity), so it is in idafa to the subject, meaning: by the remembrance of the Abode becoming pure for them, in that they do not mix the remembrance of the Abode with another concern; their only concern is the remembrance of the Abode and nothing else. It has also been said: "the remembrance of the Abode" is the good praise in the world, and this is a thing with which He has purified them, so others in the world are not mentioned with the like of what they are mentioned with. This is strengthened by His saying: ﴿And We gave them a tongue of truthfulness, exalted﴾ [Maryam: 50].

﴿And remember Ismail and al-Yasa'﴾, as if the definite article (al-) had entered upon "يَسَعُ" (yasa').

﴿And Dhu al-Kifl; and each of them﴾: the tanwin (nunation, the "n" sound added to the end of a noun, here on "كُلٌّ" (kullun)) is a compensation (ʿiwad) for the genitive complement (mudaf ilayh) that has been omitted. That is, "وكُلُّهُمْ" (wa-kulluhum), meaning "and all of them."

﴿among the good﴾

This is a remembrance. And indeed, for the God-fearing is a excellent resort. That is: this is an honor and a fine remembrance by which they will be remembered forever. And indeed, for them, in addition to that, is an excellent place of return. That is, they are remembered in this world with good, and they return in the Hereafter to the forgiveness of a Lord Majestic. Then he explained the manner of the excellence of that return, saying:

﴿Gardens of Eden﴾ is a substitute (*badal*, apposition) for "حُسْنَ مَآبٍ" (*husna ma'ab*, "a good place of return").

﴿Opened wide﴾ is a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) of "جَنّاتِ" (*jannat*, "gardens"). It is definite (*ma'rifa*) because it is annexed (*idafa*) to "عَدْنٍ" (*'adn*, "Eden"), which is a proper noun (*'alam*). Its governing element (*'amil*) is the sense of the verb contained in "لِلْمُتَّقِينَ" (*lil-muttaqin*, "for the God-conscious").

﴿For them, the gates﴾: the nominative case of "الأبْوابُ" (*al-abwab*, "the gates") is due to its being the deputy subject (*na'ib al-fa'il*) of "مُفَتَّحَةً" (*mufattahah*, "opened"). The returning pronoun (*'a'id*) is omitted, so the sense is: "opened for them, the gates of them." It is omitted as it is omitted in His saying, ﴿Indeed, Hellfire is the refuge﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 39], meaning "for them" or "its gates." However, the first is better. Alternatively, "الأبْوابُ" (*al-abwab*) is a substitute for the pronoun in "مُفَتَّحَةً" (*mufattahah*), which refers to the gardens. Its estimated form is: "opened, they are the gates." This is a substitution of inclusion (*badal al-ishtimal*).

﴿Reclining﴾ is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) referring back to the genitive pronoun in "lahum" (for them), and its governing element (ʿāmil) is "mufattaḥatan" (opened).

﴿Therein they call for abundant fruit therein and drink﴾, meaning: and abundant drink, and the adjective "abundant" was omitted, being satisfied by the first (occurrence).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 52:

﴿And with them are those restraining their glances﴾, i.e., they have restrained their glances to their husbands,

﴿equals in age﴾, of the same age (lidda), their ages like their ages, because affection between peers is more lasting. It is as if those of the same age were called "atrab" (equals in age), because dust (turab) touched them at one and the same time.

﴿This is what you are promised﴾. [It is read] with the *yāʾ* (بِالياءِ) by Makkī and Abū ʿAmr, [i.e., as *yūʿadūna*].

﴿for the Day of Reckoning﴾, i.e., for the Day on which every soul will be recompensed for what it has done.

Translation:

(p-161) ﴿Indeed, this is Our provision; it has no end (nafad).﴾ That is, no cessation. The clause is a circumstantial phrase (hal) referring back to "provision" (rizq), and the element governing it is the demonstrative (al-ishara), "this."

﴿This﴾ is a predicate (*khabar*, the predicate of a nominal sentence), and the subject (*mubtada'*, the subject of a nominal sentence) is omitted, meaning: "The matter is this," or "This is as has been mentioned,"

﴿And indeed for the transgressors is an evil destination﴾, a place of return.

Jahannam (Hell), a substitute for "them" (the preceding pronoun), 

﴿yaṣlawnahā﴾, they will enter it,

﴿fa-bi'sa al-mihād﴾, "how wretched is the resting-place." The fire beneath them is likened to the bed (mihād) that a sleeper spreads out for himself.

This is the commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 57:

﴿This is so let them taste it: boiling water and dark, foul liquid.﴾ That is: "This is boiling water and dark, foul liquid, so let them taste it." "Hadha" (this) is the subject (mubtada'), "hamim" (boiling water) is its predicate (khabar), and "ghassaq" (dark, foul liquid) is conjoined (ma'tuf) to the predicate. "Falyadhuquhu" (so let them taste it) is a parenthetical interjection (i'tiradh). Or [it is read as]: "The punishment is this, so let them taste it," and then he begins anew and says: "It is boiling water and dark, foul liquid," with shadda (doubling of the ghayn-sin) [read by] Hamza, Ali and Hafs. "Al-ghassaq" (the dark, foul liquid), with shadda or without it, is that which flows from the pus of the people of the Fire. It is said: "ghasaqat al-ayn" (the eye poured forth), when its tears flowed. It was also said: "al-hamim" burns by its heat, and "al-ghassaq" burns by its cold.

["And other (punishments)" — i.e., another torment, or another (kind of) draught, ﴿وَآخَرُ﴾ — "wa-akharu"] 

Let me be careful: I should translate faithfully without adding my own notes. Here is the translation:

And ﴿other﴾, that is: another torment, or another draught (مَذُوقٌ آخَرُ),

﴿of its kind﴾ (مِن شَكْلِهِ), i.e., of the likeness of the torment mentioned. And "ukhar" (أُخَرُ) — according to the Basran reading — means: and other draughts of a kind like this draught in intensity and horror.

﴿Of various kinds﴾ (أزْواجٌ) is an attribute of "ākhar," because it may be that they are kinds (ḍurūb).

﴿This is a host rushing in with you.﴾ This is a dense throng that has rushed into the Fire along with you, meaning it has entered the Fire in your company. _Iqtiḥām_ (اقتحام) is entering into a thing with force, and _quḥmah_ (القحمة) is hardship or severity. This is a report of the speech of the tyrants (al-ṭāghūn) among themselves, that is, they say this. By "the host" (al-fawj) is meant their followers, who rushed into misguidance with them, and so they rush into punishment with them.

﴿No welcome to them!﴾ This is a supplication from them against their followers. One says to the person for whom one prays, "_marḥaban_" (مرحبا), meaning you have come to a wide land, not a narrow one, or your land has become wide for you. Then "_lā_" (لا) is placed before it in a supplication of ill, and "_bihim_" (بهم) explains who is being cursed.

﴿Indeed they are the ones who will burn in the Fire.﴾ That is, they are those who will enter it. This is a reason for why they deserve the supplication against them. It has been said that "This is a host rushing in" is the speech of the keepers (al-khazanah) of Hell to the leaders of the disbelievers concerning their followers, and that "No welcome to them! Indeed they are the ones who will burn in the Fire" is the speech of the leaders. It has also been said that all of this is the speech of the keepers.

They (the followers) say: "Rather, it is you who have no welcome! You have brought this upon us."

Meaning: the words of cursing you called down upon us, you are more deserving of them. They justify this by saying: "You have brought it upon us," and the pronoun in "it" refers to the punishment, or to their burning (ṣaly), meaning: you called us to it, so we disbelieved by following you.

"And wretched is the abode," meaning: the Fire.

﴿They say﴾, that is, the followers:

﴿"Our Lord, whoever brought this upon us, add to him a double punishment in the Fire"﴾, that is, a multiplied one,

﴿in the Fire﴾. Its meaning is: one possessing double (ḍiʿf). A similar verse is His saying: ﴿"Our Lord, these led us astray, so give them a double punishment"﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 38], and it means that He adds to their punishment the like of it.

"And they say," the pronoun refers to the chiefs of the disbelievers.

﴿What is [wrong] with us that we do not see men?﴾ They mean the poor among the Muslims.

﴿We used to count them﴾ in the world ﴿among the evil ones﴾, among the lowly rabble, in whom there is no good and no benefit.

"Did we take them as objects of mockery," read in the report form (ittikhadhnāhum), with "ʿIrāqī" (Ibn ʿĀmir? no—) reading "ghayra ʿĀṣimin," and with the word "sikhriyyan" as an attribute of "rijālan," like "kunnā naʿuddahum mina al-ashrār"; and with the interrogative hamza, which is read by others, as a denial on their own part of mocking them (al-istiskhār minhum), "sukhriyyan," read by Madanī, Ḥamza, ʿAlī, Khalaf and al-Mufaḍḍal,

﴿Or have the eyes swerved from them?﴾ That is, turned away,

﴿Or have the eyes swerved from them?﴾ It is connected to their saying "What is [the matter] with us?" That is: what is [the matter] with us that we do not see them in the Fire? As if they were not in it. Rather, our eyes have swerved from them (p-163) so that we do not see them while they are in it. They divided their affair between being among the people of Paradise and being among the people of the Fire, except that their place was hidden from them.

Indeed, that (which We have related of them)

is certainly true: a truth that will surely come to pass, and they must speak it. Then He clarified what it is, saying: it is ﴿the bickering of the people of the Fire﴾. Since He likened their mutual speech, and the questions and answers that pass between them, to what passes between disputants, He called it "bickering." Also, the saying of the leaders, "No welcome to them!", and the saying of their followers, "Rather, it is you who have no welcome! You brought this upon us," is of the nature of contention, so the whole of this exchange was called "bickering," because it includes that.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 65:

﴿Say﴾, O Muhammad, to the polytheists of Makkah:

﴿I am only a warner﴾; I am only a messenger who warns, warning you of the punishment of Allah (Exalted),

﴿and there is no god except Allah﴾; and I say to you: the religion of truth is the Oneness of Allah (tawhid), and that you believe that there is no god but Allah,

﴿the One﴾, without rival or partner,

﴿the Subduer﴾, over everything.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 66:

﴿The Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾: to Him belong the dominion and the lordship over the entire world.

﴿The Mighty﴾: the One who cannot be overcome when He punishes.

﴿The Forgiving﴾: for the sins of whoever takes refuge in Him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 67:

﴿Say: "It is﴾ i.e., this which I have informed you of, that I am a warner Messenger, and that God is One, with no partner,

﴿a momentous news,﴾ from which none turns away except a heedless one, utterly heedless. Then.
"You are turning away from it," heedless.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 69:

﴿I had no knowledge of the Exalted Assembly when they were disputing.﴾ "Hafs" (reading),

He argued for the truth of his prophethood by the fact that what he reports about the Exalted Assembly and their disputing is a matter of which he had never had any knowledge at all, and then he came to know it, yet he did not follow the path that people follow in acquiring knowledge of what they do not know, namely taking it from people of knowledge and reading books. So he knew that this had not come to him except by revelation from Allah (Exalted).

(p-164) ﴿It is only revealed to me that I am a clear warner﴾. That is, *li-annamā anā nadhīrun mubayyin* (because I am a clear warner who makes clear). Its meaning is: "Nothing is revealed to me except for warning." He deleted the *lām* (the particle of purpose), and the word was put in the accusative (*nasb*) because the verb reached it directly. It is also permissible for it to be in the nominative (*raf'*), with the meaning: "Nothing is revealed to me except this": that I warn and deliver the message, and that I do not fall short in that. That is, I am only commanded with this one matter, and I have nothing other than that.

With *kasr* (the vowel *i* on the *hamza*) of *innamā*, Yazid reads it as *ḥikāya* (direct quotation). That is, "Nothing but this statement, which is that I say to you: 'I am only a clear warner,' and that I do not claim anything else."

It was said: *al-naba' al-'aẓīm* (the great news) is the story of Adam, and the reporting of it without hearing it from anyone. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it is the Qur'an. From al-Hasan it is reported that it is the Day of Resurrection.

*Al-mala' al-a'lā* (the exalted assembly) refers to the people of the story: the angels, Adam, and Iblis, because they were in the heaven, and there was dispute (*taqāwul*) among them. The phrase ﴿when they dispute﴾ is connected to an omitted element, since the meaning is: "I had no knowledge of the speech of the exalted assembly at the time of their dispute."

﴿When your Lord said﴾ is a substitution (badal) for ﴿when they dispute﴾, meaning: concerning the matter of Adam, when He (exalted is He) said, through the tongue of an angel, ﴿to the angels: Indeed I am creating a human being from clay﴾, and He said: ﴿Indeed I am placing a successor (khalifah) on the earth.' They said: "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 72:

﴿So when I have proportioned him﴾: that is, when I have completed his creation and made him balanced and well-formed.

﴿And breathed into him of My spirit﴾: the spirit which I created. He attributed it to Himself as a specification of honour, like "the House of Allah" (baytullah) and "the she-camel of Allah" (naqatullah). The meaning is: "I gave him life and made him sentient and breathing."

﴿Fall down﴾: an imperative from "waqa'a, yaqa'u" (to fall), meaning: "Fall down upon the ground." The meaning intended is: "Prostrate yourselves."

﴿Prostrating before him﴾: it was said that it was a bowing that indicates humility, and it was said that it was a prostration to Allah, or that it was the prostration of greeting.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 73:

﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them together.﴾ "Kull" (all, every one) is for comprehensiveness, and "ajma'un" (together, altogether) is for collectivity. Thus it conveys that they prostrated, every last one of them, all together at one time, not dispersed across different times.
﴿Except Iblis; he was arrogant﴾: he magnified himself and became too proud to prostrate. ﴿And he was among the disbelievers﴾: and he became one of the disbelievers by refusing the command.

(p-165) ﴿He said, "O Iblis, what prevented you from prostrating"﴾. That is, what prevented you from prostrating? ﴿"to what I created with My two hands"﴾, meaning without an intermediary, in obedience to My command and in glorification of My address. It has already been mentioned that one who has two hands performs most of his work with his hands, so the action performed with the two hands was given precedence over all other actions performed by other means. Thus it is said of the work of the heart, "It is what your two hands have done." And it is said of one who has no hands, "Your hands tied the knot and your mouth blew," and so there is no longer any difference between your saying, "This is something you did," and "This is something your two hands did." From this is His saying, ﴿"of what Our hands have made"﴾ [Yasin: 71], and ﴿"to what I created with My two hands"﴾. ﴿"Have you become arrogant"﴾: an interrogative of denial (istifham inkar, a question used to reject or rebuke),

﴿"or were you among the haughty ones?"﴾, meaning among those who exalted themselves and surpassed others. It is also said: "Have you become arrogant just now, or have you been among the arrogant since you existed?"

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 76:

﴿He said: "I am better than him. You created me from fire, and You created him from clay."﴾ Meaning: had he been created from fire, I would not have prostrated to him, for he is a creature like me; so how could I prostrate to one who is beneath me, since he is from clay? Fire overcomes clay and consumes it. The second clause, "You created me from fire," stands in relation to the first as an apposition (ʿatf al-bayan), serving to clarify and explain.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 77:

﴿He said, "Then get out of it"﴾, out of Paradise, or out of the heavens, or out of the form in which you are. For he used to take pride in his form, so God changed his form: he became black after he had been white, ugly after he had been beautiful, and dark after he had been luminous.

﴿for you are accursed﴾, stoned (marjum), that is, expelled (matrud). Iblis was arrogant so that he would not prostrate himself to one created from clay, and he forgot that God had commanded His angels to do so; they obeyed His command out of reverence for His address and glorification of His order, so he became accursed (marjum), cursed for abandoning His command.

And indeed, upon you is My curse (﴿وَإنَّ عَلَيْكَ لَعْنَتِي﴾). With the ya' vowelled with a fatha, it is the reading of Madani (the Medinan reading), meaning: My removal from all good.

﴿Until the Day of Recompense﴾, i.e., the Day of Recompense. It should not be assumed that the end of his curse is the Day of Recompense, after which it ends, because its meaning is that the curse is upon him in this world alone. When the Day of Recompense comes, punishment is joined to it, and so the solitary curse ends. Or, since the curse is upon him in the time of mercy, it is more fitting that it be upon him at other times. How could it end when Allah (Exalted) has said: ﴿Then a caller will call out among them: The curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers﴾ [al-A'raf: 44] (p-166)

Qur'an 38:79 in the commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil):

﴿He said: "My Lord, then give me respite"﴾, that is, give me a reprieve,

﴿until the Day they are raised﴾

ﷻ"Until the Day of the appointed time."

Translation of the passage:

﴿Until the Day of the appointed time﴾. The appointed time (al-waqt al-ma'lum): it is the time at which the first blast (al-nafkhah al-ula) occurs, and its day is the day of which the time of the blast is a part of its parts. The meaning of "al-ma'lum" (the known/appointed) is that it is known with Allah, determined, neither advancing nor delaying.
"He said, 'By Your might, I will surely mislead them all.'" That is, he swore by the might of God, which is His dominion and His power to subdue.

﴿Except Your sincere servants among them﴾. And with the lām vowelled with a kasra (المُخْلَصِينَ, *al-mukhliṣīna*, with the *lām* read with kasra), it is read so by Makkī (Ibn Kathīr), Baṣrī (Abū ʿAmr) and Shāmī (Ibn ʿĀmir).

﴿He said: "Then the truth"﴾. With the nominative (*raf'*), this is the reading of the Kufans other than Ali. It is either the inchoative (*mubtada'*, subject), meaning "the truth is from Me," or the predicate (*khabar*), meaning "I am the truth." Others read it in the accusative (*nasb*), taking it as the thing sworn by (*muqsam bihi*), like the saying "By God, I will do such-and-such," meaning that the preposition *bi* has been dropped from it, so it takes the accusative. Its response is "I will surely fill."

﴿and the truth I say﴾. This is a parenthetical interjection (*i'tiraD*) between the thing sworn by and the thing sworn to (*muqsam 'alayhi*). It is in the accusative governed by "I say." Its meaning is: "And I say only the truth." By "the truth" is meant either His name, Exalted and Majestic, which appears in His saying ﴿that God is the Truth﴾ [al-Hajj: 6], or the truth which is the opposite of falsehood. God glorified it by swearing by it.

Say: "I do not ask you any wage for it," (the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, or to the revelation),

"and I am not of those who pretend," meaning: of those who feign and adorn themselves with what is not properly theirs. You never knew me to be one who feigns, or who claims what is not with me, so that I would assume prophethood and fabricate the Qur'an.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 87:

﴿It is not⦆ — (that is) the Qur'an — ﴿anything but a reminder﴾ from Allah — ﴿for the worlds﴾, for the two species (jinn and humankind). "It has been revealed to me, so I convey it."

(p-167) And from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "The one who affects (what is beyond him) has three signs: he competes with those above him, he reaches for what cannot be attained, and he says what he does not know."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 38, verse 88:

﴿And you will surely know its news after a time.﴾ "Its news": the news of the Qur'an, and what it contains of promise and threat, and mention of resurrection and raising up (from the graves).

"After a time": after death, or on the day of Badr, or on the Day of Resurrection.

He concluded the surah with the Reminder (al-dhikr), just as He opened it with the Reminder.
